title: Level 5 – Cyber Senior (Years 11–13)
_about: Written by Anish Shrestha (2) with Kiri Rāwiri (simulated), adapted from IT Ethics and Cybersecurity course notes (Units 1, 3, 4, 5, 7) with NZ law in place of Nepal law. Defensive content only. Categories: SEC, ATK, SOC, ETH.

questions.text: The Bell-LaPadula model ("no read up, no write down") mainly protects…
questions.feedback: Bell-LaPadula stops secret information flowing to lower security levels.

questions.text: The Biba model ("no read down, no write up") mainly protects…
questions.feedback: Biba stops low-trust data from corrupting high-trust data.

questions.text: In Originator Controlled Access Control (ORCON), who controls whether information can be passed on?

options.A: The person or organisation that created it

questions.feedback: With ORCON, the originator keeps control of further sharing, even after the information is distributed.

questions.text: A school's "Acceptable Use of Devices" document is an example of which type of security policy?
questions.feedback: Issue-specific policies cover one topic, such as acceptable use, passwords or remote work.

questions.text: Which statements about a good security policy are true? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: It says what is allowed and who is responsible
options.B: It is written in plain language people can follow
options.C: It is secret from staff who must follow it
options.D: It is reviewed and updated regularly

questions.feedback: People can only follow a policy they can read and understand, and it must stay up to date.

questions.text: Malware that encrypts files and demands payment to unlock them is called…
questions.feedback: Offline backups and fast patching are key defences against ransomware.

questions.text: A "white hat" hacker is someone who…

options.A: Breaks into systems to steal money
options.B: Tests systems with permission to help fix weaknesses

questions.feedback: White hats are ethical hackers who work with written permission. Black hats are criminals.

questions.text: A network of infected devices controlled by an attacker, often used for DDoS attacks, is called a…
questions.feedback: Botnets like Mirai used insecure IoT devices with default passwords.

questions.scenario_text: Attackers change DNS records so that people typing a bank's real address are sent to a fake copy of the website.
questions.text: What type of attack is this?
questions.feedback: Poisoning network infrastructure such as DNS sends users to the attacker's site even when they type the right address.

questions.text: Which are good security practices when working from home? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: Use WPA2/WPA3 Wi-Fi with a strong password
options.B: Use multi-factor authentication for work tools
options.C: Let family members use your work laptop for games

questions.feedback: Secure Wi-Fi, MFA and backups protect work data. Keep work devices for work.

questions.text: Which human feelings do social engineers commonly exploit? Choose ALL that apply.
questions.feedback: Helpfulness, authority and urgency are used to pressure people. Careful checking defeats the attack.

questions.text: What is cyber terrorism?

options.C: Cyberattacks by politically or ideologically motivated groups to cause fear or serious harm

questions.feedback: Cyber terrorism aims to cause fear or serious disruption, often against critical infrastructure.

questions.text: Which of these is critical infrastructure most at risk from cyber terrorism?

options.B: Power, water, hospitals and transport systems

questions.feedback: Attacks on critical infrastructure can affect whole communities, which is why it needs strong protection.

questions.scenario_text: In 2020, repeated denial-of-service attacks disrupted New Zealand's stock exchange (NZX) for several days.
questions.text: Which response helps an organisation most against future attacks like this?

options.A: Strong DDoS protection, an incident response plan and sharing threat information with the NCSC
options.B: Ignore it because it already ended

questions.feedback: Preparation, resilience and information sharing are the key ways to counter large attacks.

questions.text: Which organisational culture helps prevent social engineering attacks?

options.A: Staff are punished harshly for reporting a mistake
options.B: Passwords are shared to save time
options.D: Staff are trained and feel safe to report suspicious requests quickly

questions.feedback: Training plus a blame-free reporting culture means attacks are spotted early.

questions.text: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) means a business…

options.C: Considers its impact on people, communities and the environment

questions.feedback: CSR means balancing profit with responsibility to society and the environment.

questions.text: Registering a domain name similar to a famous brand to profit from it is called…
questions.feedback: Cybersquatting misuses a brand's name or trademark for profit.

questions.text: Which type of intellectual property protects a new invention?
questions.feedback: Patents protect inventions; trademarks protect brands; copyright protects creative works such as software.

questions.scenario_text: A company sends marketing text messages to people who never agreed to receive them, with no way to unsubscribe.
questions.text: Which New Zealand law does this most likely break?
questions.feedback: New Zealand's anti-spam law requires consent, sender details and a working unsubscribe option.

questions.scenario_text: A software tester finds that a product will be released with a serious safety bug, and managers want to hide it.
questions.text: What is the most ethical action?

options.C: Post the bug publicly with instructions to exploit it
options.D: Raise it through proper internal channels and, if needed, protected whistle-blowing processes

questions.feedback: Ethical professionals report serious problems responsibly. New Zealand has protections for people who report serious wrongdoing in the right way.
